in_text_mentions: A previously healthy, immunocompetent four-year-old girl presented to the emergency department with fever, malaise and several blistering lesions that appeared after two days of pain and erythema in the neck and extremities. The lesions started as flaccid bullae that desquamated and afterwards crusted. They were localized in the neck, extremities and perioral and periorbital areas, with copious purulent secretions around the nares and eyes. All the lesions were painful and desquamated when pressure was applied (positive Nikolsky sign) (Figure 1).

in_text_mentions: ributed to by a pro-thrombotic state induced by SSSS. There was no strong indication for intensive anticoagulation, and the patient remained on his prophylactic dose of 40mg of enoxaparin twice daily based on weight (103kg) for the duration of his admission. His rash and pain subsequently improved following 48 hours of antibiotics. Formal histological results showed subcorneal and intraepidermal vesicles containing neutrophils, consistent with SSSS (Figures 2, 3). His antibiotics were rationalised, and he completed 14 days of intravenous linezolid and clindamycin with a resolution of the rash.

In Figures 2, 3, punch biopsies from the left upper arm show a spongiotic dermatitis with underlying dermal oedema and mixed inflammation. The inflammatory infiltrate contains neutrophils, lymphocytes and rare eosinophils. Karyorrhectic debris is also present. There is no evidence of vasculitis. The high-power view shows a subcorneal, intraepidermal vesicle containing neutrophils. The appearances favour infection and would be consistent with the clinical impression of staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome.

There was no strong indication for intensive anticoagulation, and the patient remained on his prophylactic dose of 40mg of enoxaparin twice daily based on weight (103kg) for the duration of his admission. His rash and pain subsequently improved following 48 hours of antibiotics. Formal histological results showed subcorneal and intraepidermal vesicles containing neutrophils, consistent with SSSS (Figures 2, 3). His antibiotics were rationalised, and he completed 14 days of intravenous linezolid and clindamycin with a resolution of the rash.

In Figures 2, 3, punch biopsies from the left upper arm show a spongiotic dermatitis with underlying dermal oedema and mixed inflammation. The inflammatory infiltrate contains neutrophils, lymphocytes and rare eosinophils. Karyorrhectic debris is also present. There is no evidence of vasculitis. The high-power view shows a subcorneal, intraepidermal vesicle containing neutrophils. The appearances favour infection and would be consistent with the clinical impression of staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A (left), B (center), C (right)). A (left): Real pediatric patient photograph from a case report titled as staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome; caption explicitly describes well-demarcated erythematous macules on the nose, chin, and forehead, consistent with the scarlatiniform erythematous phase of SSSS. Eyes masked for anonymization does not affect the visible facial eruption. B (center): Real patient photograph showing sheet-like superficial desquamation with denuded skin on the right upper chest and post-auricular area, the hallmark exfoliative finding of SSSS; in-text confirms scaling with denuded skin behind the right ear and upon the right upper chest. C (right): Real patient photograph of blanching erythematous macules on the dorsal trunk, matching the erythematous rash of SSSS; in-text notes macules on the trunk. Disease attribution is supported by the SSSS case-report title and the specific captioned manifestation.
